question: Against a backdrop of growing geopolitical instability and attacks on multilateralism, the EU’s credibility is based on common rules, scientific evidence and effective protection of public interest. However, the repeated use of omnibus packages raises doubts over legal certainty, regulatory quality and respect for environmental protection and public health objectives.

The environmental omnibus includes simplification proposals that affect key instruments, such as environmental impact assessments, the Industrial Emissions Directive or chemical transparency tools. In addition, it has been announced that the Water Framework Directive will be revised and simplified in 2026. 1.
How will the Commission prevent the automatic presumption of ‘overriding public interest’ from rendering the Water, Birds and Habitats directives and the Nature Restoration Regulation meaningless?
How does the Commission justify the weakening of the Industrial Emissions Directive or the scrapping of the SCIP database, which are key to risk prevention?

In relation to the announced revision of the Water Framework Directive, how will the Commission ensure a rigorous and independent impact assessment that preserves environmental and health protection objectives, particularly the principle of nondeterioration?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.4.2026) The omnibus package1 aims to reduce administrative burdens and reporting obligations while streamlining environmental procedures. It does not seek to affect the environmental objectives of the underlying legislation.

The Commission proposal provides2 that certain projects in strategic sectors or categories shall be considered to be of public interest and may be considered to have an overriding public interest and to serve public health and safety3. Member States may restrict this application to certain territories, types of technology or projects with certain technical characteristics.

Competent authorities will need to assess projects on a case-by-case basis to consider their ‘overriding’ public interest and the absence of alternative solutions. Regarding the Industrial Emissions Directive4, its core elements remain unchanged, with Commission proposals focusing on simplification without compromising its objectives.

The Substances of Concern in articles or in Products (SCIP) database has been considered ineffective and costly, as waste operators struggle with its complex information requirements. Regulation (EU) 2025/24555 (One Substance One Assessment) introduces the Common Data Platform on Chemicals, which will incorporate data from the SCIP database.

Regarding the revision of the Water Framework Directive6, in line with the Better Regulation Guidelines7, the Commission will conduct a proportionate impact assessment and consultation process ensuring that proposals are evidence-based. A call for evidence has been launched8.
